I would interpret this in a completely different way…

Start of turn and end of turn are phases, because multiple effects happen at this specific time of the turn, and never simultaneously. Play a card, use a power, draw a card are not phases, but "points in time", a given event with no duration.

You could say that the player's turn is made of three "phases" : start, actions, end, each with (possibly) multiple events happening in a given order.

Don't remember where it is on this forum, but I think I remember seeing that when ruling that cards saying "at the start of turn you may decide to skip your turn", you could chose when exactly in the order of event you decided to stop the start of turn resolution and skip.

Correction : you don't "choose" when to skip, you skip when the order cards were played activates the card that gives you the choice. It still means that the "start of turn" phase ends then, and other effects "stacked" to happen, don't.

By default, the "action" phase has three different actions that always happen in the same order : play card, use power, draw card, but individual cards and powers can cause other events/actions to happen, you can play a card that has you use a power or draw a card, etc.

You seem to see "start of turn" and "end of turn" as triggers with no duration, while I understand them as a sequence of event. Funny how the same rulebook can lead to very different way to understand what happens

posts.name: dypaca
posts.cooked:
The verb tense on Spite's healing ability is different from other damage reaction abilities, so you wouldn't be completely out of line to argue another interpretation.  But I think it makes the most sense to do the damage first, then the healing which is triggered by it.

For your new questions, now we are getting into the territory of abilities which react when something would be dealt damage and redirection (which is different from reacting to damage which is dealt).  I'm a bit less confident that my answers are backed up by official rulings here.

For the first question, Mr Fixer takes 3 damage.

For the second question, he could redirect the damage.  She would do only 1 damage to the new target, assuming there are no other modifiers.  (There was an interesting ruling that ANY two cards which share nemesis icons are nemeses, meaning she would have the damage boost if it is redirected to the Chairman).

More generally, when damage is redirected resolve it as though the new target were the original target.  (The only exception to this is smoke bombs which redirects and modifies the damage).  Like I said, I don't know of a statement directly from the designers supporting that, but I think it is the correct way to play.

I feel that it contradicts the general "keep it simple, super-stupid" design ethos of SOTM for there to be a distinction between "damage dealt by" and "damage dealt to".  If someone is immune to damage, then damage was not dealt to them.  In a game like Magic the Gathering, you draw distinctions between those kinds of things, but MTG is a game where you can "combo out" to deal functionally infinite amounts of damage by exploiting a rules loophole; SOTM should not function the same way.

While players are within their rights to "cheat" for their own amusement, I believe that they should not be permitted to claim the bragging rights for a victory which they achieved by playing fast and loose with the rules.  In order for their win to be meaningful, it should have been strict-RAW-legal.  And in particular, I don't believe it should be possible to report victories on the Statistics Thread which were in any way "tainted" by laxity in enforcing the villain's (or environment's) destructive power against the players.  Doing so distorts the perception of how powerful a certain hero or how difficult a certain villain really is.
